title: The freedom of a Christian
hookLine: Luther: a Christian is free lord of all, and dutiful servant of all

cards: Two sentences, side by side, that seem to cancel each other out. A Christian is a free lord of all, subject to no one. A Christian is a dutiful servant of all, subject to everyone.

Martin Luther, whose hammer you met in year one, set those two at the top of a short book called The Freedom of a Christian, and spent the rest of it showing why both are true at once. Free and bound. Lord and servant.

teach.b: Luther's freedom starts somewhere unexpected: not with what a person does, but with what a person receives.
For Luther, someone is made right with God by faith, by trusting God's promise in Christ, not by piling up good works. That's the lord-of-all half.
In Luther's telling, nothing a person fails at can take away what God has given, and nobody is working to earn their place.
So the Christian is free. Then comes the turn. Free for what?

Luther's answer: for the neighbor. Because Christians don't need good works to save themselves, they can give those works away. Works stop being a ladder you climb and become a gift you hand across the fence.
He took the pattern from Paul: "For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all." And again: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another."
To the Galatians, Paul puts both halves in one breath: "ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another."

Luther even pictures a Christian becoming a kind of Christ to the neighbor, giving freely as Christ gave. Christians describe faith and works in different ways. Lutheran churches follow Luther closely here.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians also teach that grace comes first and that love must act, while explaining how faith and works fit together in their own terms. In each of them, the neighbor still gets served.

how: Lutheran and other Protestant Christians read Luther's treatise as a classic statement of faith and freedom; across churches, Christians practice service to neighbors through charity, volunteering, and ordinary acts of care.

games.q: what does “the freedom of a christian” mean?
o: free to do whatever you like, with no duty to others
free from church rules by obeying every civil law
free through faith, and a servant of all through love

games.q: free and a servant — tap the pairs.
p: owe no man any thing, but to love

s: Luther said Christians are free, so they owe nobody anything
he said both: free lord of all, and dutiful servant of all.
Luther drew the two sentences from Paul
"though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all."
in Luther's picture, good works are a ladder to climb to God
faith receives; good works become a gift handed to the neighbor.

games.q: a friend has just heard that nothing anyone does can earn God's love; it's a gift. they ask: so why bother doing good at all? what would Luther say?
o: "you don't need to; faith is enough, so stop."
"because you're free, you can give your good works to your neighbor."
"do them to make sure you're really saved."
games.why: free lord of all, through faith; dutiful servant of all, through love. good works stop being a ladder and become a gift.

practice: Bring to mind one small service for someone who can't pay you back and might not even notice: a neighbor's bin, a coworker's extra task, the dish someone left in the sink.
Watch where your mind goes, will they thank me, will it count, and let those questions drop, picturing it done out of freedom, with nothing to earn. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: The freedom of a Christian. Luther's two sentences: free lord of all, through faith; dutiful servant of all, through love.

orig.note: Greek, Galatians 5:13: liberty, the freedom Paul says Christians are called to, and then told to use in love.

carryVoice: Your line: free and a servant. Free by faith, a servant by love. See you tomorrow.
